---
title: "Classifying Texts with tidyllm"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE)
options(width = 90)
```

You have thousands of short free-text answers and a fixed list of categories. A language model can label each answer in minutes. A single label can differ from run to run, though, and a label that comes back every time can still be wrong.

Here you write a codebook (a definition for each category), label every answer several times, and compare the runs. You send the answers where the runs disagree through a stronger second pass and check the result against a sample of answers coded by people.

A faster, cheaper route is a *decision model*, a different kind of model that you call with `decide()` instead of `chat()`. It answers a closed question such as "which of these 23 codes?" with the code and a probability, and writes no text. The section "An alternative: decision models" runs it on the same sample.

Chunks that call an API (a model provider's web service) are not evaluated; the next chunk loads the saved results, so you can follow along without an API key, the password for that service. If you rerun them, they cost money. The [Get Started](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm.html) article has a table of where to get a key for each provider.

## The task

Seven thousand survey respondents described their job in their own words, which gives 2,209 distinct answers, since many people use the same words (for example "lawyer"). We sort each answer into one of 22 two-digit groups of the SOC (Standard Occupational Classification, the US scheme for job categories), or into code 99 when it names no occupation.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyllm)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)

occ_data  <- read_rds("occupation_data.rds")
occ_codes <- read_rds("occ_codes_2digits.rds")

distinct_occupations <- occ_data |>
  distinct(occupation = occupation_open) |>
  mutate(id = row_number())

print(distinct_occupations, n = 5)
```

We classify each distinct answer once and join the labels back at the end.

## Why a single answer is not enough

In 2026, most paid providers no longer let you set `temperature`, the setting that controls how much a model's answers vary for the same input. Most current paid models reject it. OpenAI and Claude models return an error, and recent Gemini models, including the default of `gemini()`, accept it and ignore it. `provider_capabilities()` lists which providers accept it.

So you cannot make a model repeat itself, and the same prompt on the same text can return different labels, mostly on borderline texts (Barrie, Palaiologou and Törnberg, 2024; Haldar and Hockenmaier, 2025). The remedy is the one used with human coders: label each answer several times, compare the runs, and check the labels against a validation sample, a set of answers coded by people (Pangakis, Wolken and Fasching, 2023).

The chat examples use `claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5")`.

## Step 1: Write a codebook, not a list

A codebook gives each label a definition, a rule for overlaps and one or two examples. Without one the model guesses what "Management" or "Missing" covers.

```{r codebook}
codebook <- read_file("classifier_codebook.txt") |> trimws()
cat(codebook)
```

Keep the codebook in a file under version control. Rerun step 6 after every edit, so the accuracy you report matches the codebook you use.

## Step 2: Constrain the answer with a schema

Asking for "only the code" breaks `parse_number()` when the model adds a word. A schema, a fixed list of fields the reply must fill, avoids this. `field_fct()` makes the label an enum, a field that takes only values from a fixed list. We add a one-sentence rationale to read when you audit a row and a three-level confidence to sort by.

```{r schema}
label_levels <- as.character(c(occ_codes$occ2, 99)) |> unique()

occ_schema <- tidyllm_schema(
  name       = "occupation_label",
  rationale  = field_chr("One sentence: which words in the answer decide the group."),
  occ2       = field_fct("The SOC two-digit group from the codebook.", .levels = label_levels),
  confidence = field_fct("How clear the answer is.", .levels = c("low", "medium", "high"))
)
```

```{r prompt_fn}
make_prompt <- function(occupation, codebook) {
  llm_message(glue(
    'You code survey answers into occupation groups.
     Use only the codebook below. Choose the single best group.
     If the answer names no occupation, use 99.

     Codebook:
     {codebook}

     Survey answer: "{occupation}"'
  ))
}
```

A dry run, `.dry_run = TRUE`, shows the request that would be sent without sending it, so you can check it before spending anything.

```{r dry_run, eval = FALSE}
make_prompt(distinct_occupations$occupation[1], codebook) |>
  chat(claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", .json_schema = occ_schema, .dry_run = TRUE))
```

Heavy output constraints can cost accuracy, the share of answers where the model's label equals the human label, on hard cases (Tam et al., 2024); the rationale field is there for that reason.

One call looks like this:

```{r one_call, eval = FALSE}
make_prompt("Doin' the numbers", codebook) |>
  chat(claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", .json_schema = occ_schema)) |>
  get_reply_data()
```

`get_reply_data()` returns a named list with one element per schema field. The label stays a character string, because "99" and "11" are labels.

## Step 3: Label every answer several times

We ask for each answer `k` times and keep every run. Three runs give a majority; five give a finer agreement score at a higher price. We use a random sample of 150 distinct answers.

`parallel_chat()` sends the requests concurrently and returns one reply per prompt, in the same order.

The chunk below builds one ready-to-send prompt per answer and run and keeps it in a `prompt` column next to the answer.

```{r repeat_tasks, eval = FALSE}
k <- 3

sample_df <- distinct_occupations |>
  slice_sample(n = 150)

tasks <- sample_df |>
  cross_join(tibble(run = 1:k)) |>
  mutate(prompt = map(occupation, make_prompt, codebook = codebook))
```

```{r repeat_run, eval = FALSE}
replies <- parallel_chat(
  tasks$prompt,
  claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", .json_schema = occ_schema),
  .max_active = 4
)
write_rds(replies, "runs_claude.rds")
```

Failed requests do not stop the call; `parallel_chat()` warns how many failed, and you can run those prompts again.

`get_reply_data()` turns the list of replies into a tibble with one row per reply, in the same order: `reply_id`, `error` and one column per schema field. A failed request keeps its row with the message in `error`. The chunk lists those rows in `failed`, so you can run them again, and drops them from `runs`.

```{r tidy_runs, eval = FALSE}
reply_data <- get_reply_data(replies)

failed <- filter(reply_data, !is.na(error))

runs <- tasks |>
  bind_cols(reply_data) |>
  filter(is.na(error)) |>
  select(id, run, label = occ2, rationale, confidence)
```

The saved results hold three labels for each of the 150 sampled answers.

```{r load_runs}
sample_df <- read_rds("classifier_sample.rds")
runs      <- read_rds("classifier_runs.rds")
run_meta  <- read_rds("classifier_runs_meta.rds")
run_tokens <- run_meta$tokens |>
  rename(prompt_tokens = input_tokens, completion_tokens = output_tokens)

runs |>
  left_join(sample_df, by = "id") |>
  select(id, occupation, run, label, confidence) |>
  print(n = 6)
```

Tokens are the short pieces of text a model reads and writes, and providers charge by them. `get_metadata()` returns one row per reply with its `prompt_tokens` and `completion_tokens`:

```{r repeat_meta, eval = FALSE}
run_tokens <- get_metadata(replies)
```

The codebook is part of every request, so prompts are far longer than the answers. We count them for the 450 saved calls.

```{r tokens}
run_tokens |>
  summarise(
    calls               = n(),
    prompt_per_call     = round(mean(prompt_tokens)),
    completion_per_call = round(mean(completion_tokens)),
    prompt_tokens       = sum(prompt_tokens),
    completion_tokens   = sum(completion_tokens)
  ) |>
  relocate(calls, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens)
```

### The same job as a batch

For a full dataset where a result an hour later is fine, `send_batch()` submits the same list as a batch, a job you collect later, at half the price. `check_batch()` reports the status and `fetch_batch()` returns the replies. We sent the first 20 requests as a test; the chunk submits the batch job, checks it, fetches the replies and reads them with `get_reply_data()` as before.

```{r batch_variant, eval = FALSE}
first20 <- slice(tasks, 1:20)

job <- send_batch(first20$prompt, claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", .json_schema = occ_schema))
write_rds(job, "runs_batch_job.rds")

job <- read_rds("runs_batch_job.rds")
check_batch(job, claude())

replies <- fetch_batch(job, claude())

batch_runs <- bind_cols(first20, get_reply_data(replies))
```

The two `check_batch()` outputs come from right after submission and three minutes later:

```
# A tibble: 1 x 8
  batch_id          status      created_at          expires_at          req_succeeded
  <chr>             <chr>       <dttm>              <dttm>                      <int>
1 msgbatch_017iBx1… in_progress 2026-10-02 13:22:40 2026-10-03 13:22:40             0
# i 3 more variables: req_errored <int>, req_expired <int>, req_canceled <int>

# A tibble: 1 x 8
  batch_id          status created_at          expires_at          req_succeeded
  <chr>             <chr>  <dttm>              <dttm>                      <int>
1 msgbatch_017iBx1… ended  2026-10-02 13:22:40 2026-10-03 13:22:40            20
# i 3 more variables: req_errored <int>, req_expired <int>, req_canceled <int>
```

The batch reported 27,823 prompt tokens for 20 requests, about 1,390 each, matching the live calls. Its labels compare with the first live run:

```{r batch_results}
batch_runs <- read_rds("classifier_batch_results.rds")

batch_runs |>
  select(id, occupation, label = occ2, confidence) |>
  inner_join(
    runs |> filter(run == 1) |> select(id, live_label = label),
    by = "id"
  ) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), same_label_as_live_run = sum(label == live_label))
```

### Using more than one model

A second model shows whether two independent systems read the codebook the same way. Agreement across models is the stronger signal, because unrelated models fail less alike (Ziems et al., 2024). Running the same prompts through another provider adds its labels as extra runs. We did not run this here.

```{r second_model, eval = FALSE}
replies_gemini <- parallel_chat(tasks$prompt, gemini(.json_schema = occ_schema), .max_active = 4)
```

## Step 4: Summarise agreement and flag disagreements

The next chunk counts the votes per label, puts the most-voted label first, and keeps it with its vote share. The `unstable` flag marks answers where the runs disagree.

```{r vote}
vote <- runs |>
  count(id, label, name = "votes") |>
  arrange(id, desc(votes)) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(
    n_runs     = sum(votes),
    majority   = first(label),
    agreement  = first(votes) / sum(votes),
    candidates = paste(label, collapse = "/")
  ) |>
  left_join(sample_df, by = "id") |>
  mutate(unstable = agreement < 1)

vote |>
  count(unstable) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
```

Almost every answer gets the same label in all three runs. The rows where the runs differ form a short list to read; step 6 shows it catches only part of the errors.

A tie, such as one vote each for three labels, has no majority and `first()` picks one arbitrarily, so treat rows with `agreement < 0.5` as unresolved. A unanimous label can still be wrong.

Krippendorff's alpha scores agreement beyond chance, with 1 as full agreement. Here the raters are the runs and the units the answers. The helper `kripp_nominal()` computes it for nominal labels and returns one number; its code sits in a hidden chunk in the source of this page.

```{r helpers, echo = FALSE}
kripp_nominal <- function(runs) {
  m <- runs |>
    select(run, id, label) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = id, values_from = label) |>
    select(-run) |>
    as.matrix()
  m  <- m[, colSums(!is.na(m)) >= 2, drop = FALSE]
  lv <- sort(unique(as.vector(m)))
  o  <- matrix(0, length(lv), length(lv))
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(m))) {
    v   <- m[, j]
    v   <- v[!is.na(v)]
    tab <- table(factor(v, lv))
    o   <- o + (tab %o% tab - diag(tab)) / (length(v) - 1)
  }
  n <- sum(o)
  1 - (n - 1) * (n - sum(diag(o))) / (n^2 - sum(rowSums(o)^2))
}

cohen_kappa <- function(truth, estimate) {
  lv <- sort(unique(c(truth, estimate)))
  tb <- table(factor(truth, lv), factor(estimate, lv))
  po <- sum(diag(tb)) / sum(tb)
  pe <- sum(rowSums(tb) * colSums(tb)) / sum(tb)^2
  (po - pe) / (1 - pe)
}
```

```{r alpha}
kripp_nominal(runs) |>
  round(3)
```

Rules of thumb call 0.8 reliable and 0.667 the lowest value for tentative conclusions (Krippendorff, 2004). Alpha measures agreement between runs only; human labels come in step 6.

### Self-reported confidence

Does the confidence field carry a signal? We check against the maintainer's labels for the 150 answers, made with AI assistance and checked by hand (step 6). We call them gold labels: the labels a person assigned, which we treat as the truth to compare against.

```{r load_gold}
gold <- read_rds("classifier_gold.rds")

scored <- vote |>
  left_join(gold, by = "id") |>
  mutate(match = majority == gold)

runs |>
  left_join(select(scored, id, match), by = "id") |>
  group_by(majority_matches_gold = match) |>
  summarise(runs = n(), share_low_confidence = mean(confidence == "low"))
```

Runs on rows where the majority label disagrees with the human label are much more often marked "low". The field helps rank rows to read, but many mismatched rows still carry "medium" or "high".

### Token probabilities, where the provider offers them

Some providers report how likely each piece of the reply (each token) was, so the probability of the label token is a free confidence score. `openai()` and the Chat Completions based providers accept `.logprobs` and `.top_logprobs`; `claude()` has no such argument. They describe one run of one model and say less with structured output, where the label sits inside a JSON string. Decision models avoid that limit; see the next section.

## An alternative: decision models

`decide()` sends the text and a closed question to a decision model, a model that returns the chosen code and a probability (a score between 0 and 1) for every code, with no text. It is much faster and cheaper than a chat model. The [decision models article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_decide.html) explains the question types and providers; here we use one choice question.

The codebook becomes the question. In R a choice question is a factor and its possible answers are levels: each level is an occupation code, described by its codebook line. `field_fct()` takes the codes as `.levels` and the descriptions as `.level_descriptions`.

This reads the codebook file, one line per code, and splits each line into a code and a description.

```{r decide_question}
codebook_levels <- tibble(line = read_lines("classifier_codebook.txt")) |>
  filter(str_trim(line) != "") |>
  separate(line, c("code", "description"), sep = " ", extra = "merge")

occ_questions <- tidyllm_schema(
  name = "occupation_label",
  occ2 = field_fct(
    "The SOC two-digit occupation group of this survey answer.",
    .levels             = codebook_levels$code,
    .level_descriptions = codebook_levels$description
  )
)
```

`decide()` takes the text in `.state`, the questions in `.questions` and a provider. One line before each answer says what the text is; without it, `openai()` labelled answers such as "Doctor" as code 99 ("no occupation").

```{r decide_one, eval = FALSE}
frame_answer <- \(x) paste0("Survey question: What is your job? Answer: ", x)

decide(frame_answer("Residential roofer"), occ_questions, gemini()) |>
  select(question, type, answer, probability)
```

```
# A tibble: 1 x 4
  question type   answer probability
  <chr>    <chr>  <chr>        <dbl>
1 occ2     choice 47           0.998
```

Code 47 is Construction and Extraction, which fits a roofer. A list of texts in `.state` returns one row per text and question. We run the 150 human-labelled answers of step 4 through `jev()` (the provider of the Jev decision model), `openai()` and `gemini()`; the three runs took 6.9, 10.5 and 7.7 seconds. In the next chunk, `label_all()` runs one provider over all 150 answers and joins the human labels; the `list()` call does this for the three providers.

```{r decide_run, eval = FALSE}
label_all <- function(provider) {
  res <- decide(as.list(frame_answer(sample_df$occupation)), occ_questions, provider)
  sample_df |>
    mutate(label = res$answer, probability = res$probability, probs = res$probabilities) |>
    inner_join(gold, by = "id")
}

decide_runs <- list(jev = label_all(jev()), openai = label_all(openai()), gemini = label_all(gemini()))
write_rds(decide_runs, "classifier_decide_runs.rds")
```

```{r decide_load}
decide_runs <- read_rds("classifier_decide_runs.rds")
decide_all  <- bind_rows(decide_runs, .id = "provider")
```

First-pass accuracy against the human labels, next to the majority of the three Claude runs from step 4:

```{r decide_accuracy}
claude_row <- scored |>
  summarise(provider = "claude, majority of 3 runs", answers = n(),
            correct = sum(majority == gold), accuracy = round(mean(majority == gold), 3))

decide_all |>
  group_by(provider) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), correct = sum(label == gold), accuracy = round(mean(label == gold), 3)) |>
  bind_rows(claude_row)
```

All three decision models reach 0.83 to 0.84, level with the Claude majority, in seconds and with one call per answer instead of three. The table below groups the answers into probability bands. Each cell shows the share labelled correctly and, in brackets, the number of answers in the band.

```{r decide_bands}
decide_all |>
  mutate(band = cut(probability, c(0, 0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 1), include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(provider, band) |>
  summarise(cell = str_glue("{sprintf('%.2f', mean(label == gold))} ({n()})"), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = provider, values_from = cell, values_fill = "0 rows")
```

Above 0.95, 96 to 100 percent of the labels match the human label; below 0.5, fewer than half do. At a cut-off of 0.8, rows at or above it are right 93 to 96 percent of the time and rows below it 51 to 62 percent. Send the rows below the cut-off to a person or to step 5.

```{r decide_flagged}
decide_all |>
  mutate(flagged = probability < 0.8) |>
  group_by(provider, flagged) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), correct = sum(label == gold), accuracy = round(mean(label == gold), 2), .groups = "drop")
```

The three providers are independent readers of the codebook, so the agreement logic of step 4 applies. `openai()` and `gemini()` choose the same code for 88 percent of the answers, `gemini()` and `jev()` for 87 and `openai()` and `jev()` for 82. All three agree on 119 of the 150 answers, and 92 percent of those match the human label. The 31 others are a short list to read by hand.

A decision model returns no reason; use the `chat()` pass of step 5 for rows that need one. Its labels are only as good as the codebook, so steps 6 and 7 apply here too.

### Hierarchical codes with a beam search

The 22 groups are the top level of a taxonomy, a tree of categories with subcategories. Real codings, such as occupations or industries, go several levels deeper with hundreds of codes, and one question with that many levels is too long for the model to read well. The TypeSafe documentation calls the remedy a beam search: ask a choice question at the top level, keep the few top-scoring groups, ask a second question inside each, and continue down. A path scores the product of the probabilities along it, and you keep the few best paths at each level. The `probabilities` column holds one probability per code, including the runners-up.

A small example: for one answer, level one gives codes A 0.6 and B 0.3. Inside A the best child scores 0.5 and inside B 0.9. The paths score 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.30 and 0.3 × 0.9 = 0.27, so keep both.

The chunk below takes the answer where `jev()` is least sure and lists its three highest-probability codes.

```{r decide_top3}
doubtful <- decide_runs$jev |>
  slice_min(probability, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

enframe(doubtful$probs[[1]], name = "code", value = "probability") |>
  slice_max(probability, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(occupation = doubtful$occupation, probability = round(probability, 3), .before = 1)
```

A beam search would carry these three codes into the next level.

tidyllm has no helper for this yet, and we did not run a full beam search on this two-digit example. A deeper codebook needs a few lines of `decide()` and `map()` on top of the code above.

## Step 5: Reclassify the disagreements

Rows where the runs disagreed or any run said "low" get a second look. Instead of voting again, we show a more capable model the answer, the earlier labels and their rationales, and turn reasoning on.

```{r reclassify_prompt}
make_review_prompt <- function(occupation, rationales) {
  llm_message(glue(
    'Earlier independent attempts coded this survey answer; they disagreed or were unsure.
     Decide using the codebook. If the answer is genuinely too vague to place, use 99.

     Codebook:
     {codebook}

     Survey answer: "{occupation}"

     Earlier labels and reasons:
     {rationales}'
  ))
}
```

The next chunk adds the earlier labels and rationales to each flagged row, sends the rows to the stronger model and reads the replies as before.

The next chunk keeps the answers where the runs disagreed or any run said "low".

```{r reclassify_select}
to_review <- runs |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(any_low = any(confidence == "low")) |>
  left_join(vote, by = "id") |>
  filter(unstable | any_low)
```

```{r reclassify_run, eval = FALSE}
rationales <- runs |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(rationales = paste0("- ", label, ": ", rationale, collapse = "\n"))

review_prompts <- to_review |>
  left_join(rationales, by = "id") |>
  mutate(prompt = map2(occupation, rationales, make_review_prompt))

review_replies <- parallel_chat(
  review_prompts$prompt,
  claude(
    .model       = "claude-opus-5-5",
    .json_schema = occ_schema,
    .thinking    = TRUE,
    .max_tokens  = 4000
  ),
  .max_active = 4
)

reviewed <- review_prompts |>
  bind_cols(get_reply_data(review_replies)) |>
  select(id, review_label = occ2, review_rationale = rationale, review_confidence = confidence)
```

Keep `.max_tokens` generous with reasoning on, since thinking tokens count against it.

```{r reclassify_load}
reviewed <- read_rds("classifier_reviewed.rds")

tibble(
  flagged_rows        = nrow(to_review),
  runs_disagreed      = sum(to_review$unstable),
  only_low_confidence = sum(!to_review$unstable),
  reviewed_rows       = nrow(reviewed),
  same_ids            = setequal(to_review$id, reviewed$id)
)
```

This keeps the review label where there is one and the majority label otherwise, and tags each row as unanimous, reviewed or human queue.

```{r final_labels}
final <- vote |>
  left_join(reviewed, by = "id") |>
  left_join(gold, by = "id") |>
  mutate(
    occ2   = coalesce(review_label, majority),
    source = case_when(
      !is.na(review_label) & review_confidence == "low" ~ "human_queue",
      !is.na(review_label)                              ~ "reviewed",
      TRUE                                              ~ "unanimous"
    )
  )

final |> count(source)
```

The review changed the label of a few rows:

```{r review_changes}
final |>
  filter(!is.na(review_label), review_label != majority) |>
  select(occupation, majority, review_label, gold, review_confidence)

tibble(
  changed       = sum(final$review_label != final$majority, na.rm = TRUE),
  reviewed_rows = sum(!is.na(final$review_label))
)
```

The review is a second opinion from the same model family and can repeat a shared misreading. Rows the reviewer marks as low confidence go to a human queue:

```{r human_queue}
final |>
  filter(source == "human_queue") |>
  select(occupation, candidates, review_label, gold)
```

## Step 6: Validate against human labels

Only human coding shows whether labels are right. Draw a random sample across all answers, since flagged rows alone make the estimate too pessimistic. One or two people code it from the same codebook without seeing the model labels and resolve their differences. Do not tune the codebook on this sample and then report it as your accuracy.

The 150 answers here were coded with AI assistance and checked by hand by the maintainer. Code 98 in the original file, for answers that name no occupation, was recoded to 99 to match the codebook. The comparison turned up four labels where the model was right and the first hand label was wrong; we corrected them before the numbers below.

We compute accuracy and Cohen's kappa, the agreement with the human labels beyond what chance gives, in base R. Kappa helps with 22 groups of very different sizes, where frequent classes dominate accuracy. The helper `cohen_kappa()` is in the same hidden chunk; the table compares the first run, the majority and the majority plus review.

```{r metrics}
first_run <- runs |>
  filter(run == 1) |>
  select(id, first_run = label) |>
  inner_join(gold, by = "id")

bind_rows(
  first_run |>
    summarise(pipeline = "first run only", accuracy = mean(first_run == gold), kappa = cohen_kappa(gold, first_run)),
  final |>
    summarise(pipeline = "majority of 3 runs", accuracy = mean(majority == gold), kappa = cohen_kappa(gold, majority)),
  final |>
    summarise(pipeline = "majority plus review", accuracy = mean(occ2 == gold), kappa = cohen_kappa(gold, occ2))
) |>
  mutate(accuracy = round(accuracy, 3), kappa = round(kappa, 3))
```

The three rows are close, because the model gave the same label in nearly all runs from the start. The review touches only the hardest answers:

```{r review_effect}
final |>
  filter(!is.na(review_label)) |>
  summarise(rows = n(), before_review = mean(majority == gold), after_review = mean(occ2 == gold))
```

About one final label in six does not match the human label. The table shows which route the mismatches took:

```{r errors_by_source}
final |>
  group_by(source) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), mismatches = sum(occ2 != gold), accuracy = mean(occ2 == gold))
```

Where do the mismatches come from?

```{r mismatches}
final |>
  filter(occ2 != gold) |>
  arrange(gold) |>
  select(occupation, model = occ2, human = gold, candidates) |>
  print(n = 30)
```

Two groups dominate. The model gave vague answers such as "Keep things organized", "Workforce Optimization" or "Buildin and fixin things" code 99, because the codebook says to prefer 99 over a guess, while the human placed them from context. For slang or terse answers such as "Private dick", "I haul" and "Barster" the model guessed a group and the human coded 99. Some answers fit two groups under the codebook: whether bakery work is production (51) or food service (35), where "Lead mechanic supervisor" belongs, and whether massage is healthcare or personal care.

More runs would not average these errors away. Most are rows where the model gave the same label every time, so step 3 cannot find them.

Compare the model with the agreement between two humans on the same sample: if two careful coders agree 0.85 with each other, a model at 0.85 matches them. A model's quality depends on the task, codebook and data, so check it each time (Gilardi, Alizadeh and Kubli, 2023; Pangakis, Wolken and Fasching, 2023). Only one human checked the labels here, so the 83% comes with that limit.

Check also whether errors are spread evenly: if one group or phrasing carries most of them, a downstream estimate can be biased even when overall accuracy looks high. The validation sample can also correct for misclassification.

```{r errors_by_group}
final |>
  group_by(human_group = gold) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), accuracy = mean(occ2 == gold)) |>
  arrange(accuracy, desc(answers)) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)
```

## Step 7: Do not tune the codebook on your validation sample

The mismatch table invites an edit to the codebook, so we made one. Version 2 adds a rule for bakery and food batch work (51 unless it is retail counter work), puts massage under personal care (39), counts lead and supervisor titles and general operations work as management (11), and counts electrical and mechanical upkeep as installation and repair (49). We labelled the 150 answers three more times with it.

```{r codebook_v2_run, eval = FALSE}
codebook_v2 <- read_file("classifier_codebook_v2.txt") |> trimws()

prompts_v2 <- tasks |>
  mutate(prompt = map(occupation, make_prompt, codebook = codebook_v2))

replies_v2 <- parallel_chat(
  prompts_v2$prompt,
  claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", .json_schema = occ_schema),
  .max_active = 4
)

runs_v2 <- prompts_v2 |>
  bind_cols(get_reply_data(replies_v2)) |>
  select(id, run, label = occ2, rationale, confidence)
```

The next chunk compares the majority label of each codebook version with the human labels, on the sample we wrote the edit from:

```{r codebook_v2_sample}
runs_v2 <- read_rds("classifier_runs_v2.rds")

sample_comparison <- bind_rows(v1 = runs, v2 = runs_v2, .id = "codebook") |>
  count(codebook, id, label) |>
  group_by(codebook, id) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  inner_join(gold, by = "id") |>
  group_by(codebook) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), accuracy = mean(label == gold))

sample_comparison
```

We wrote the edit while looking at these errors, so this gain is expected. To test the new codebook, we labelled 292 further distinct answers once with each codebook. These held-out answers were set aside and never used to build or change the codebook; the chunk that builds them takes a `heldout` table of these answers, and the next one loads their saved labels from `classifier_heldout_runs.rds` and the human labels from `classifier_heldout_gold.rds`.

```{r codebook_heldout_run, eval = FALSE}
codebooks <- tibble(codebook = c("v1", "v2"), text = c(codebook, codebook_v2))

heldout_prompts <- heldout |>
  cross_join(codebooks) |>
  mutate(prompt = map2(occupation, text, make_prompt))

heldout_replies <- parallel_chat(
  heldout_prompts$prompt,
  claude(.model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", .json_schema = occ_schema),
  .max_active = 4
)

heldout_runs <- heldout_prompts |>
  bind_cols(get_reply_data(heldout_replies)) |>
  select(id, occupation, codebook, label = occ2, rationale, confidence)
```

```{r codebook_heldout}
heldout_runs <- read_rds("classifier_heldout_runs.rds")
heldout_gold <- read_rds("classifier_heldout_gold.rds") |>
  mutate(gold = ifelse(gold == "98", "99", gold))

heldout_comparison <- heldout_runs |>
  inner_join(select(heldout_gold, id, gold), by = "id") |>
  group_by(codebook) |>
  summarise(answers = n(), accuracy = mean(label == gold))

heldout_comparison
```

On the held-out answers version 2 is slightly worse than version 1: the edits fitted the quirks of the 150 answers. Tune on one part of the human-labelled answers and report on another, or label a fresh sample after every round of edits.

## Cost and size

The token table in step 3 gives the numbers for one prompt: about 1,400 prompt and 77 completion tokens. The next chunk multiplies the average tokens per call by the number of calls and the price per token:

```{r scale}
per_call <- run_tokens |>
  summarise(prompt = mean(prompt_tokens), completion = mean(completion_tokens))

price_input  <- 2
price_output <- 10

tibble(
  distinct_answers  = nrow(distinct_occupations),
  runs              = 3,
  requests          = distinct_answers * runs,
  prompt_tokens     = round(requests * per_call$prompt),
  completion_tokens = round(requests * per_call$completion),
  usd_standard      = round((prompt_tokens * price_input + completion_tokens * price_output) / 1e6, 2),
  usd_batch         = usd_standard / 2
)
```

The prices are those of `claude-sonnet-5-5` on 2026-10-02: 2 USD per million input tokens and 10 USD per million output tokens, half through the batch API ([Anthropic pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing)). At these rates the 450 calls behind the three runs cost about 1.60 USD, the second pass with `claude-opus-5-5` (4 and 20 USD) about 0.20 USD, and the step 7 codebook experiment about 3.90 USD.

A decision model sends a shorter request: about 675 prompt tokens per answer with `openai()`, against about 1,400 for the chat prompt, and the reply is a code and a probability. The full 2,209 answers take under two minutes per provider at the speed measured above.

## What to take away

- Label each answer several times and estimate how stable the model is.
- Measure agreement between runs, and check accuracy against human labels. Here three runs gave the same label for nearly every answer, and about one in six of the final labels still differed from the human label.
- Write a codebook with definitions and decision rules. It does more for agreement than any prompt trick, and most remaining errors sit there.
- Use `field_fct()` to restrict labels to the codebook, and check accuracy in step 6.
- Use a decision model as the quick alternative: one call per answer, a probability for every code, and on this sample the accuracy of three Claude runs. Use the probability to pick rows to review.
- Repeat the call, vote and read the rows where runs disagree. Send those through a stronger second pass and keep a human queue for the rest.
- Validate on a random, held-out, human-coded sample, and report agreement with the number of coders behind it. Check the human labels as carefully: validation found four errors in ours.
- Tune the codebook on one set of answers and validate on another.
